title: How Fine Grinding Optimizes the Antioxidants and Aroma of Blueberry Pomace
metaDescription: Discover how particle size in grinding blueberry pomace affects its phenolic compounds, color and aroma profile, according to science.
excerpt: A study analyzes how micronizing blueberry pomace changes its microstructure, optimizing the release of phenolic compounds and boosting its fruity and toasted aromas.
imageAlt: Fine blueberry pomace powder in a bowl next to whole fresh blueberries.

blocks.text: Introduction: making use of blueberry pomace

Processing fruit such as blueberries generates valuable by-products that are often underestimated in the food industry. One of these by-products is blueberry pomace, the fibrous material left after juice extraction or primary processing. This dry residue is rich in bioactive compounds and has a characteristic fruity aroma profile, making it a promising ingredient to enrich a variety of foods. However, to get the most out of its qualities, science studies grinding and micronization technologies that make it possible to modify its physical microstructure. Understanding how this ingredient reacts when it is ground to different particle sizes is key to determining the best way to preserve its sensory properties and its natural antioxidants.

As science explores new techniques to add value to these by-products, it becomes clear that grain size not only changes the visual appearance but directly alters how phenolic compounds interact with their environment. Recent research published in the journal Foods investigates exactly these microscopic dynamics, evaluating the porosity, pore volume and thermal behavior of blueberry pomace powder at different grinding levels.
What the source says: the impact of particle size on pomace

The research evaluated the effect of applying coarse and ultrafine grinding to blueberry pomace, producing powders with five different particle sizes spread over three clear structural scales: the plant scale (particles larger than 500 micrometers), the tissue scale (between 100 and 500 micrometers) and the cell scale (between 10 and 100 micrometers). Through microscopic analyses and correlations, the researchers observed that an intermediate grinding, between the tissue scale and the cell scale, increased the porosity of the particles and reduced their size, which significantly improved the ability to release the phenolic compounds present in the material.

However, the study identified an important limitation during the process: when grinding reached the cell scale (particles of 10 to 100 micrometers) for a prolonged time, the total phenolic content decreased. The authors attributed this reduction to thermal degradation caused by the friction and heat during intensive grinding. On the other hand, through the analysis of the aroma profile, the team identified a total of 45 volatile organic compounds (VOCs). It was observed that the cell-scale grinding enriched both fruity and toasted aromas. This phenomenon was directly linked to the increase in pore volume (PV) and specific surface area (SSA), together with the decrease in particle size. In addition, grinding increased the lightness and red hue of the powder compared with the control sample. Weighing microstructure, functional components, aroma and color, the researchers concluded that the preferred method to process blueberry pomace is a 20-minute grinding, so that most particles have a size between 10 and 100 micrometers, with a small proportion retained between 100 and 200 micrometers.

These findings fit with what food science has been observing about the physics of plant matrices. Reducing particle size in fruit powders increases the contact area with the surrounding medium, making it easier to extract or release beneficial substances such as phenolic antioxidants. However, this laboratory test shows that there is a technical balance point: grinding too much can generate excessive heat that chemically degrades the very compounds one wants to protect. Therefore, understanding these physical dynamics makes it possible to design industrial processes that optimally preserve the sensory attributes of color and aroma without sacrificing the nutritional value of the plant material.
What it means for you: application in food development

For consumers and the ingredient-development industry, these data are a clear guide on how to make the most of blueberry by-products as flour or functional powder. Although the study was done as a laboratory test with processed pomace, it suggests that texture and grinding level in dehydrated ingredients can change the perception of aroma (making it more fruity or toasted) and improve the availability of their bioactive compounds. Understanding the balance between thermal processing and physical refinement helps choose processed products of better aromatic and nutritional quality for smoothies, baking or cereal blends.

The study shows that a controlled 20-minute grinding of blueberry pomace achieves the ideal combination of phenolic release, intensified fruity aromas and improved color lightness.
